utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge May is indisposed today. The Chamber will continue sitting under Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, yesterday we interrupted your testimony during your recounting some of your work on the exchange of bodies commission. I'd like to begin this morning by showing you a document, and it is Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 14. And I'm going to ask that you be shown both the original B/C/S and the English translation. I'd ask you to take a look at the original B/C/S document before it's placed on the overhead projector, and after you've had a chance to look at it, I'd ask you to tell us whether or not you recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was handed to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who handed you this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My CO, Colonel Bulat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when was it that Colonel Bulat gave you this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that I received it on September 25th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And has that document been in your possession until you turned it over to the Office of the Prosecutor here at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To save a bit of time, I'm going to ask you -- it's a short letter. I'm going to ask you to take a look at the English translation and read it. If there's any part of that translation that does not comport with your understanding of the document, or you disagree with any portion of the translation, I'd ask you to indicate that and to tell us what you believe the document to say. So I'd ask you now to read this translation of that document for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republic of Srpska Krajina, Main Staff of the Serbian army, confirmation number 15-440 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the -- slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. "Republic of Srpska Krajina. Main Staff of the Serbian Army. Confirmation number 15-440, 29th of September, 1994. Meeting of war prisoner exchange commissions. To be delivered to the 21st Corps (war prisoners exchange commission). "Since the war prisoners exchange commission of the 1st Krajina Corps made an appointment to meet with a similar commission of the so-called ABiH, it is necessary that the representatives of your commission attend, too, and that they tell the Turkish commission openly that we, (RS and RSK), are one people, but that on the paper we are divided in two states. "From the intelligence service obtain a few names of the most extremist members of the 5th Corps of the so-called ABiH, and convey them to the Turkish commission. Tell them that we have around 3.000 of their members that are in prison, not in a refugee camp. You have to let them know that we are not in the position to beg, but that we are those who are setting the conditions up. "It should be checked whether there are relatives and friends of the leading military and politicians from c. Krajina among the prisoners and convey their names to them, too. "Assistant Commander Colonel Marinko Gajic." And then there's a stamp on the bottom of the original document, received on the 29th of September, 1994, at 1530, processed at 1530, and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does that translation accurately reflect the contents of the original Serbian document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you now to assist the Chamber in placing that document in context, and I want to ask you a few specific questions. The reference to RS and RSK and "are one people," what did that -- can you put that into context? What was the author of this letter indicating by that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, indicating that the Serbs on both sides of the frontier then, between the Republic of Srpska and Republic of Srpska Krajina are all Serbs, serving in one army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The portion of the letter which indicates that the Serbs have around 3.000 members in prison camps, not refugee camps, is that -- do you have knowledge whether that 3.000 were simply military soldiers that had been captured or were they also civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to be honest and admit that I am not aware of the 3.000 being held anywhere in RSK, which I cannot claim for the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, were there 3.000 soldiers anywhere within the 21st command's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last paragraph, when it talks about checking whether there are relatives and friends of leading military and politicians, can you indicate or describe for us what that meant, place that in context for us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant very simply that if we did held anybody that was important to the other side, they should be used as a blackmail tool.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were attempts made to identify the people in custody to determine if they were related to any prominent members of the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those we held in prison have been severely questioned to establish whether there are any relationships to the leading political figures in B and H.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there ever any attempts to identify people related or friends of prominent members who were not yet in custody, to identify them and place them in custody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge in RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now draw your attention to May 1995, and ask you: Did you have occasion to see an order regarding the shelling of the frontier or front line near Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Order issued by the President Martic was issued to all the commands of all the corps and at one of the briefings in the morning it was read to all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise to the usher. I'm finished with that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this order issued by President Martic, can you please describe what you recall about it when it was read out in the morning briefing.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, it stated that any case of provocation from the Croatian side or any attack from the Croatian side, all the corps deployed along the frontier from north to south should be burning on the other side, meaning that the artillery attack would immediately begin all along the frontier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based on your experience and participation in that morning briefing, is it your belief that Mr. Milosevic had anything to do with this particular order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After -- strike that. Was this order ever implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one instance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there any reaction to its implementation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The unit that have opened the rocket fire on Zagreb was immediately arrested and removed from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know who arrested them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special police from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how much time transpired between the rocket attack and the arrest of the people who perpetrated the rocket attack by the special police from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it took more than six hours after.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the period of time in the Krajina in 1995. And before I ask you specific questions about that period of time, I would ask you to describe generally to the Chamber what life was like among the remaining Serb population in the Krajina in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would have to say that life was very difficult at the time. Suddenly the supplies have somehow become less and less regular as they were before. A lot of civilians have already left the area on the pretext of going to see relatives in Serbia or whatever the reason they gave. But the people started trickling away very slowly. There were a lot of rumours going around that a Croatian attack is imminent, that we are prepared to defend every inch of the soil of the RSK. It was a war of psychosis, very, very carefully built up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the level of violence or crimes that were non-conflict related in the Serb community at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to read the surveys carried on official basis by the army and losses that we have suffered at that particular moment in time. 80 per cent of those losses were contributed to ourselves and 20 per cent to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That means that the official statistic on who caused these crimes, who perpetrated these crimes, 80 per cent was attributed to Serbs themselves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now Operation Storm and ask you to describe what Operation Storm was and where were you when Operation Storm commenced?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation itself started on the morning August 5th, 1995. However, we have been informed about a pending attack two days prior, in every detail; about the time, the strength, and direction of the attack, which made me believe that we have sufficient time to regroup or increase the defence of the border itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How did you -- sorry. How did you learn about the details of the attack prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through my connections with ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you pass that information on to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within minutes of receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us who you passed this information on to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally, first was given to Colonel Bosanac who was then in charge of the 21st Corps, and then I myself personally sent a telex to Knin General HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And based on your experience of having lived in this area for several years, it was your opinion that there was a response that could be taken to these attack plans?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 5th of August, there was a first attack carried by the Croatian air force, actually, in the vicinity of the HQ of the 21st Corps, where I was at the time. However, the rockets released by these airplanes didn't come nowhere near to the actual HQ. I think they were directed to the HQ of the special police in Petrova Gora. Whether they hit it or not, I really don't know. At the same time, the infantry attack came from the direction of Petrinja and from the direction of Karlovac. The combat actually started on the ground itself by 8.00. At the same time, I was informed to go immediately back to the HQ of the UN, as if UN didn't know about the attack. I mean, I was supposed to go there and file a complaint about the attack from the Croatian side. I did get back to the HQ. Of course, the sector commander was aware of the attack and he was trying, through his own channels, to convey a message to the Croatian side via the HQ in Zagreb of the UN for the immediate ceasefire which, unfortunately, did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lazarevic, before you describe more detail about the attack, I'm going to ask you to briefly describe for the Chamber the location of the 21st Corps, the 15th Corps and the 39th Corps, all of the ARSK army. Can you please describe their relative positions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have mentioned before how narrow that section of RSK is between the B and H and Croatia. The RSK was caught kind of in the middle. And the attack was carried out on the 5th of August from both sides of the border, meaning we were attacked from behind by the 5th Corps and up front by considerable Croatian forces. The depth of the section that we defended is around 15 kilometres. The width is around 70. Considering that my eastern flank was held by the 39th Corps, which is the Banija Corps, and on my western flank Lika, or the 15th Corps, was supposed to hold the position. However, by the 9th of the 5th, in the early morning hours of the 6th, we have discovered that both of those flanks have withdrawn, that actually we have been left alone in the middle. By that time, we were already surrounded by the Croatian side. There were in Glina, and on the other side, they were in Vojnic, so there was no way out for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to the 15th Corps withdrawing, was -- was the 21st Corps made aware of that fact, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not being aware of any movement of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to the 39th Corps being withdrawn, was the 21st Corps made aware of their withdrawal, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the same thing; we were not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to the 7th of August, 1995. Were you personally present when a series of phone calls were made from the 21st Corps to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting actually took place in the HQ of the UN. We used the satellite phones in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did the UN permit you to use these satellite phones or can you explain the circumstances under which you used the satellite phone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We rented the space from the UN. We were paying 5.000 Deutschmarks a day to use this particular office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this an official agreement with the UN or was it a deal that was worked out with an individual?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a deal worked out with an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Please tell us about the phone calls that you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office, at the time when it was painfully obvious that we were sacrificed as a corps, we tried to establish contact with the General HQ in Belgrade and with the cabinet of Mr. Milosevic. In the office at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the time, it was myself, Toso Pajic, Colonel Bulat, Djuro Skaljac, and maybe one or two other persons present. The calls were made in the following order: First it was placed to the General HQ of Belgrade, General Perisic personally by Colonel Bulat. I have to say that the public announcement system was plugged in, so actually we could all listen to the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So we're clear: So the phone was on speakerphone and all people in the room to hear both sides of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the contact was established with the General HQ, Colonel Bulat has given a report as a commanding officer from the war part of the country to the General Perisic and then he asked him for advice, explaining that we have been caught and encircled totally by the enemy forces, which were considerably stronger than we were, and asked him what does he want us to do, whether to surrender, whether to fight or what. General Perisic answered with one word, and that was "Persevere", and put the phone down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did General Perisic offer any concrete assistance to the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except, "Persevere." That was about all that he said at the end of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there another phone call made that morning or that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next phone call was made to President Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who made that phone call?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pajic made that call.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you please describe the contents of that phone call.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, he explained the situation and asked for advice. Again we received exactly the same answer, that was, "Persevere."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did President Lilic offer any concrete assistance to the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there another phone call made that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Toso Pajic made one more call, and that was placed to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us the substance of that call?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, explaining the situation, development over the last 24 hours above ground, and again we heard the same reply: "Persevere." At that particular moment in time, we all looked at each other and had a feeling like these three people are in the same room even though that we have had three different telephone numbers that we have used, but the answer was exactly identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did Mr. Stanisic offer any concrete assistance to the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just before you continue, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lazarevic, you said that they were considerably stronger than you were, than your forces were. Could you put that in terms of numbers for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our estimate at the time was that we had approximately 4.000 men under arm, and I'd like to point out that none of those were professional soldiers within the RSK. Most of them actually civilians just being drawn into the conflict. At the back of us, we had a full 5th Corps of the B and H army which at the time numbered around 20.000. The both flanks, the eastern and the western flanks, the attack carried by the Croatian forces would approximate the same number of 20.000 together. In real terms, we had about 40.000 people attacking approximately 4.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did members of Arkan's Tigers receive concrete assistance during this time period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 6th of August, they have pulled out, not only Arkan's, but special forces of the Ministry of Interior of Serbia have pulled out from the area, from Pauk and from Petrova Gora with assistance of the MP Battalion from the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you be more specific about the type of assistance that the special forces from Republic of Serbia MUP and Arkan received when they withdrew from the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion of the MPs from the 21st Corps has served as a security and led the way in withdrawal of the forces from Pauk and Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge regarding who issued the order to give them protection when they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did something happen to Luna rockets that were present in the RSK at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those rockets were removed on the day when Zagreb was shelled, so we had no rocket system at the time of the attack, even though I have to admit the Croatian side was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to continue with what happened after this period, and I'd ask you to maybe describe for us what, if any, media campaign existed at this time regarding what was going to happen to the people in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, at the time of this attack, I'm now specifying the period of 6th and 7th of August, there were a lot of rumours running around, and of course all sides used it to their own benefit. The fact of the matter is that the 21st Corps left their position of Turanj and pulled all the way back to the actual compound of the UN, which we have surrounded and placed civilians between us and the UN. What I'm trying to picture to you, gentlemen, is that in any situation when aerial attack by the Croatian air force, the UN HQ would suffer considerable damage as well. That was the idea for proximity of our own troops there. At the time, we controlled a perimeter of around 7 kilometres. That was what was left of the RSK. Within this perimeter, as I said before, we had 4.000 Serbs armed and approximately 20.000 civilians. There was no food, no water, no electricity. All the other sectors had been deserted by then. Knin was taken over by the Croatian forces. The Croatian forces have advanced even further. They were approximately two kilometres away from Topusko on either side of the road, meaning from the east and from the west, and the 5th Corps has actually stopped at the border to Croatia, so they have not penetrated into the territory. If you would draw a circle around the compound of the UN, it would be probably around two and a half kilometres wide. That's about it. We have tried many things to inform the general public about the attacks of the Croatian. The information which we received from the field were that atrocities have been started by the advancing enemy forces. One particular information I have conveyed to the CNN via the satellite phone about the attack of the Croatian air force and the members of the 5th Corps on the refugee convoy which was trying to penetrate the territory into Bosnia, withdrawing from RSK. That would happen on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that story covered on CNN?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I have personally, not only me, but a number of us was watching TV at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning -- the morning of the 7th, it was already obvious that we cannot expect any assistance from anybody. We all firmly believed that we have been sacrificed so that somebody in Belgrade would gain some points after we have all met with our demise, being surrounded. Three of us at the time in the office, Colonel Bulat, myself, and Mr. Toso Pajic, have discussed the possibility. The least one liked by all three of us was actually going and commit mass suicide by counterattacking the forces which are approximately 8 to 1. Also taking into consideration that the position of ourselves would also contribute to the considerable killing of the UN personnel as well. At that time we made a decision between three of us to get in touch with the command in Zagreb via sector commander in Topusko and suggest that if we were to surrender to the Croatian side, the condition would be that we are permitted to go back to Serbia, for the convoy being escorted by the UN and ECMM and military observers, and withdraw all the way to Serbia. Finalising of this idea came after we all disagree that would not be very wise actually to travel in vicinity of the 5th Corps because the 5th Corps would not be a part of this agreement which we are about to make with the Croatian side. So we have decided actually to travel the length of Croatia with the convoy and enter Yugoslavia at Sid area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's Yugoslavia in Serbia, I mean Serbia -- the Serbian part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. On the morning of the 8th, all the details were finalised. The attacks have stopped in the meantime. The deal was that we first surrender the heavy weaponry - tanks, artillery pieces - and then along the way to relieve ourselves from all the other weapons. So approximately after about 25 kilometres on the road from Topusko, already deep in Croatia, past Petrinja, we were to surrender all the rest of the weaponry. Only officers were allowed to keep assigned weapons, but that was a kind of part that even Croatia didn't keep, they just took all the weaponry. In all fairness, I have to admit, it was a horrible convoy, very long, with approximately 25.000 people in the convoy. The length of the convoy would probably be around 30 kilometres because you had cars, tractors, horse-drawn vehicles, and it was moving extremely slow. The only part -- the only part that we have considered to be actually threatened is when we left Glina and it was -- the convoy was passing through a couple of destroyed Croatian villages at the beginning of the conflict, and it was like a gauntlet of the Croatian army alongside of the road; the distance between each of the soldiers probably about two to three metres. And us being already disarmed but still in uniform, we didn't feel very comfortable when they started checking their weapons. I suppose it was just a kind of trying to install fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, before you continue, can you give us some idea about the composition of this convoy? Is it just military members of the 21st Corps or are there also Serb civilians taking part in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy was of a mixed nature. There were military and civilians. And the civilians were not only from Topusko. Actually, there were a lot of civilians coming from deeper within Krajina, like the Slunj area, then further down. As they were pulling back or pulling out from their own position, they would actually end up in Topusko because Topusko was like, you know, the end of the road, because we were -- by then, we were already surrounded from all sides. So the convoy itself would be, as I said, approximately numbering 24.000 bodies, out of which 20.000 were civilians; you know, elderly people, ladies, kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this convoy reached the border of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was approximately a fifth car in the convoy, so I was about among the first ones to reach the actual border between Republic of Croatia and Yugoslavia. I was asked by Toso Pajic and by Colonel Bulat to stay behind -- two police officers, our own police officers, and two police officers from the Croatian side and just to check the number of the people as they are going through, which took about eight to nine hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate number of the people that passed from Croatia into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all honesty, I have to say that we've been on the road for approximately 72 hours, so that part was totally unclear to me. I know I have been writing names down. I was asked to write just the first names of the people, no surnames, no ranks, no whether they belonged to the army or not. It was just a kind of verification that the Croatian side had asked to have, at the end of the day, confirmation of all the people that have gone across if our side would claim later on that the number of people were taken out of the convoy and maybe taken to a prison or being shot or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate that number for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I stood there and about 15.000 people have gone through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would be 15.000 people, both civilian and military?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Would you please observe pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, can you now describe what you observed on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbian side of this border.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been first to get there, but I was approximately the last one to leave Croatia at the end tail of the convoy. As soon as they have crossed the road, I parked my car in Yugoslavia this time, and I slept in the car beside the road for about four to five hours. When I woke up, I decided to continue towards Belgrade. As soon as I have reached the highway known as Bratstvo-Jedinstvo, or Brotherhood and Unity Highway, this is when you encounter the first toll booth like set up before you enter the highway. On this side, on this side facing Croatia, actually, there were units of the police from Serbia stopping all the vehicles in convoys and searching them thoroughly, including the persons within the vehicles. Anything that resembled anything to do with the military was immediately confiscated and taken away. On the other side of the ramp, they had set up a little Red Cross station with fresh water, milk for the kids, bread, and things like that. But you can imagine the slowness of the process if each individual car or vehicle or pedestrian, even, being totally searched before we actually can reach the other side and have a glass of water or glass of milk. So it was a very painful and slow process. Most of the people in the convoy had been protesting vigorously against the Serbs because we just couldn't figure out if Croatia decided not to search the convoy for 72 hours as we moved through Croatia, why is it suddenly that we have to be searched so thoroughly by our own police? Nevertheless we had to put up with it, and after finally making it through the gate and entering the highway, we started moving toward Belgrade. I was driving a Mercedes at the time, so I had the opportunity to move faster than most of the convoy, meaning that I have reached Belgrade ahead of the rest of the convoy that was very slow moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what, if anything, you observed at the exit ramps to the highway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment we reached Belgrade, the exit ramp of the highway was blocked off by the police and all the traffic was directed further south. As the convoy moved further south, every other exit was also blocked off by the police, so the convoy actually had to keep on moving without stopping anywhere. The general direction of this movement was Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if a person who had fled the Krajina had family in Belgrade and wanted to stay with them, were they permitted to do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were those people being forced to go?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, along the highway, deeper south, general direction of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were there any representations made regarding what awaited the refugees down in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing. You had just a bunch of police at every exit, showing the movement of the convoy to continue down the highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time -- strike that. Did you travel on the highway through Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were able to get off of the highway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, I was moving much faster than the rest of the convoy, and those that have left the Croatia before I did, obviously had moved even further up front. So there was a section of the road that I was driving now that had no convoy in front of me or no convoy behind me, and I reached vicinity of Krusevac, where I have spotted an exit which was not guarded by the police, and this is when I swung off the road and left the highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without telling us the name of the person you went to or their relationship to you, did you go somewhere when you were able to get off of the highway?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Straight to the house of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at this person's house?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24 hours before the police showed up at the front door.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the police that showed up, were they ordinary, uniformed Republic of Serbia police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to get dressed up and leave with them to the police station. I have repeatedly asked why, and they said, "Well, we have no answer for you, but the commander of the station will inform you." When I was taken by these two police officers to the station, there were a number of people from Krajina around the station already, mostly women and children crying their eyeballs out because all the men were put on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you identify yourself and your position to the police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. Actually, there was -- in the room which was questioning every individual where is he from, there was a member of the state security with the police commander, to whom I have identified myself, given my military booklet, my driver's licence, my ID, to establish the fact that actually I am not from Krajina, that I was born in Belgrade, therefore I'm a citizen of Yugoslavia. And this gentleman from the state security told me, "Okay. You turn around and you go home now." I asked if I can use the phone so I can call the people to come and pick me up because the police brought me down. These people turned up around 3.00 in the morning and took me away. Unfortunately, the very same day in the early hours of the morning, around 10.00, the police turned up at the gate again and took me away again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where were you taken this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Straight to Krusevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you taken there alone or with other people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a bus load of us going to Krusevac who were there, and I believe there was some kind of either school or something like that, because there was a couple thousand people already. It was like a gathering centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what happened at that location?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people held in this location were all people from RSK of military age, meaning from like age of 18 to about 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were loaded on the buses there. Each bus had an escort of four police officers, including the driver. Each bus was full of people, only sitting, nobody standing but, I mean, every seat was taken by an individual. I think we left around noon, as this huge convoy of buses taking us somewhere. When we tried to establish some sort of a conversation with the police officers on board the bus, they simply would not answer where we are being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you approximate for us the number of buses in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the convoy that left with me was approximately 12 buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you perceive that you were free to get off this bus if you wished?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely nobody was allowed to leave the bus, not even go to the rest room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We kept on driving and it was getting dark, and we still didn't know which direction we are going. At one point, the lights from the bus have shown a road sign which was Dalj on this road sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you please spell that for us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: D-A-L-J.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We realised - some of us that knew - that we actually are going to the Arkan's camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was Arkan's camp located at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you -- did there come a time when you did eventually arrive at Arkan's camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived there. The whole camp was in total darkness. However, there were a number of people standing and yelling the names of the people on the bus, because obviously they were supplied with the names by the convoy leader or whoever gave them the names. And as the people were descending from the bus, they were sent to run through a gauntlet of Arkan's Tigers, who were beating them at the time as they were running through. At the time that somebody called my name, I stepped off the bus but immediately somebody walked up to me in the dark and -- somebody who recognised me or somebody who knew me -- and pulled me aside and said, "No, you don't go that way. You're not one of them," meaning I'm not a Croatian Serb but being a Serbian Serb, even though myself personally didn't make a distinction as such. And I was taken around the gauntlet, straight to the office of Colonel Pejovic and Captain Sarac, which I knew from a previous encounter in the RSK, and they were aware that I am originally from Belgrade, so I was kind of put aside, so I didn't go through this severe beating on arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you come to learn the purpose of these men being brought, these Serb men being brought to Arkan's camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently somebody had an idea that these people need to be retrained by Arkan, and that was like original virgins, whatever, brought there. I find out later on that Arkan has been paid 100 Deutschmarks per head of the Serbian brought in for retraining. The situation within the camp were atrocious. People were severely mistreated on a daily basis, property were taken away from them, their IDs were taken away from them; they have become just numbers. I'll give you instances: For example, there were three telegraph poles in front of Arkan's HQ to which every single day there were at least three Serbs chained to the post and anybody who went past can beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us how it was you learnt that Arkan was being paid to retrain these men.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very same night when I arrived to -- I will freely use "concentration camp," because that's what it was. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very same evening that I arrived to the camp, myself, I had seen a JNA officer, which I have approached and identified myself and asked for a location of the commander of the 21st Corp or any corps of the RSK. I was told by this gentleman that a joint command has been formed in Vukovar and that he will inform the necessary officers about my being held in this in this concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you explain your characterisation of this place as a "concentration camp"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, there were no freedom of movements. The whole camp was surrounded by barbed wire. It was heavily guarded by the armed men. People were mistreated 24 hours a day, beaten up severely, made to carry huge rocks, about the size of a human with the weight of approximately 60 or 80 pounds, and at any given time if they dropped this rock, they would be beaten again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learnt the purpose of this retraining? What was to happen to these men after they had been trained by Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was they will be pushed up front to fight the Croatian forces again, but this time at the back of them they would have Arkan units who would shoot them in the back if they decide to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, did there come a time when you were able to secure your own release from this camp, using your own contacts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the fifth day, a vehicle came from Vukovar joint command to take me away from this camp, and I was taken there. At this time, when I walked in the command, I was very, very disappointed. I just couldn't believe that the Serbs can do to the Serbs what they were doing, and I have asked immediate discharge from the forces. I was told to go and see Colonel Karan, who was in charge of internal security KOS, and he suggested, he said, "Well, I can't give you this discharge. What I can give, I give you a pass to go to Belgrade, and then you don't have to come back. You can go for medical check-up, just don't come back." I said, "This is not the way I want to leave the army, not by deserting it," I said, "I want a full discharge." I requested a vehicle from the command to take me straight to the Ministry of Defence of the RSK, and I went there and I raised -- I tell you, gentlemen, I did raise hell over there to get a discharge, which I eventually did, and then I sat on the first bus back to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your time at the camp, did Arkan himself address the group?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each group -- I have to tell you that every day the buses Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were coming. This is not just my convoy when it came, but on a regular basis, everybody morning and every evening, another bus load and another bus load of these poor people would come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us, during the time you were there, how many people, how many Serbs altogether you saw?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over a period of four days, at least two and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us what Arkan said to your particular group.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he lined up the group and then told them: "For the five years [Realtime transcript read in error "five days"] we have supplied you with weaponry, we have supplied you with food, with the manpower, with the officers, and yet you wouldn't even fight, in the end."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when he used the word "you," did you take that to be a reference to those people in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Lazarevic at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, how long did you stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stayed there for five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what was your treatment generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was regular treatment. I mean, nobody bothered me whatsoever. I was just put aside over there, waiting for somebody to come and pick me up from the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said something in the earlier part of your testimony today that I'd like to ask you about. Having made three phone calls to Belgrade and on each occasion you were told to persevere, your assessment was that somebody wanted to sacrifice you to score points. I think that was the term that you used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we believed, by the answers which we have received and a silent refusal of any assistance whatsoever, whether it was air force or ground troops or -- that we left there, leaving us open to try and mount a counterattack and die in the process. A lot of civilians would have been killed. The media could use that as pointing out that the Croatian side is no different than the Serbian, or even worse than the Serbian side in committing these atrocities against the civilians and the unarmed population in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe there's an error in the transcript. Before we get too far ahead, I'd ask that maybe the stenographers check it. It's on page 25, line 17. I believe the witness said five years, and it's been recorded as five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That correction will be made. Mr. Milosevic, your turn for cross-examination. I ask you, when you're cross-examining to avoid, as best you can, speeches, questions which are too long. Make your questions as short as possible. Avoid narratives and concentrate on asking short questions. You have about four hours and 50 minutes, which you do not have to use. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson, especially for this warning to take care how much time I will use up

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see from your statement that you claim that as a very young man you started working for the KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That dates back to 1968, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This activity of yours was never interrupted until the end of the war --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it continued until 1999.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From 1968 to 1999?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be precise: Until the 22nd December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And all this time, from 1968, you filed your reports to a person by the name of Nikola Zimonja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, "for the most part"? Did you file reports to someone else as well, but reports to him were regular?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How frequent were your reports to him in this entire period, from, let's say, 1968 to 1992, when I see that you joined the army of the Serbian Krajina? At the time you were a liaison officer and your activity was more intensive. But how often did you submit reports to Mr. Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minor correction: When I put on the uniform in December 1991, I put on the uniform of the JNA, not the army of the Serbian Krajina. And the reports were as frequent as my assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in terms of time, how frequent, how regular, were these reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1998, my reports were at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that period. I'm talking about from 1968 to 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regularly, without interruption, throughout those years?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were periods when I didn't file any reports at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long were these periods?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some that lasted a year, a year and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were those years when you filed no reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to remember when precisely, but let's say in 1985, 1986, or in 1983 there were regular reports during the Winter Olympics, and in 1979 I didn't submit any reports at all. What I'm trying to say is that I drew up reports if I had anything specific to report. I didn't make any contact if there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. You joined the army in end 1991, and later, in the beginning of 1992, if I understood you correctly, you were already part of this corps commanded by Colonel Bulat, which was, as you describe here, the 21st Corps of the army of the Serbian Krajina, Republic of the Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning of your testimony yesterday, you explained that Colonel Bulat had direct contact with Perisic, without strictly adhering to his vertical chain of command with the headquarters of the Serbian Krajina army; he went straight to Perisic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said in my testimony was that he had direct contact with Colonel Perisic along the line, which was a direct connection between the 21st Corps and the headquarters in Belgrade, and along another line he had contacts with the headquarters of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the office when he made his phone calls to Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were those occasions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that comes to mind first was the one that related to the joint attack with the 5th Corps of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1993. It is also fair to say that there were several attacks of this kind, so I don't remember now what specific attack it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Lazarevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the transcript I note that Mr. Perisic is referred to as "Colonel"; is it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he's a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Perisic. It was in line 8 of page 29. Okay. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from 1992 until 1993, you never heard Bulat speaking to Perisic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with my own ears. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this happened in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sincerely believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it in 1994 and 1995, since you later described these events as happening in these years?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was one of the earlier attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Earlier attacks. And it was 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only trying to establish a time frame for the events you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The attack was on the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You started working for KOS of your own free will, didn't you? You said that you accepted this work after your discussion with this person Nikola Zimonja, in your youth, and that's how had you started your work as a spy. Did that happen of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. In fact, I was very enthusiastic when I started working. I was delighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you imagine it was not difficult to find out that even Nikola Zimonja himself, at the time when he engaged you, as you say, was a student himself and had nothing at all to do with the KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. He was introduced to me as the lieutenant of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who introduced him that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My own father did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't know he was a student; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So you saw Nikola Zimonja for the first time in 1968; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You see, I have a piece of information here that tells me that you met Nikola Zimonja for the first time in 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite an incorrect piece of information, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to test it, see if it's right. You explained to me a moment ago that up until 1991, except for the pause you made in 1984 and then one year of pause later on, you sent in your reports regularly to Zimonja. Do you happen to know, for example, that Nikola Zimonja, from 1971 up until 1980, was undergoing education in the former Soviet Union? Does that mean that you sent those reports to him to the Soviet Union in that nine-year period, from 1971 to 1980?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. I would send in my reports to the Yugoslav Embassy and they were to further hand them on. The reports probably went to somebody else, because I would never hand in my reports to Mr. Zimonja personally. I would leave the reports in the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you a very specific question. I asked you who you sent your reports to, gave them to, and you said yesterday all day that you gave them to Zimonja. Now you say that you sent them in to Zimonja, and when I ask about that nine-year period and tell you that he was doing some education in the Soviet Union, you said that you did not give them to Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the reports that I sent in were addressed to Zimonja. Now, who was getting those reports, I don't know. I thought they were going to Zimonja. Whether anybody was authorised to take the reports over on behalf of Zimonja, I can't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So many things that you claimed yesterday throughout the whole day in fact I suppose you base them on assumptions, like you do this particular fact and point, or perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a characterisation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a characterisation of Mr. Lazarevic's evidence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. He's certainly entitled to ask him about specific facts that he believes the witness assumed, but certainly to make a broad statement that everything that the witness said was based on assumptions I believe is an improper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think it's really a question. It was more a comment. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to respond to the opposite side, Mr. Robinson, because if I were to present generalised statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have dealt with it. I have told you to continue. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say, Mr. Lazarevic, that he, and I'm thinking of Zimonja here, in 1990 was nominated the military attache to Czechoslovakia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mr. Zimonja you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to what Mr. Zimonja told me, that he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As he was appointed military attache in 1990, then, how can you claim that Zimonja was at a meeting with you in 1991 in Vojnic and Samarica at the beginning of 1992, when he was in fact the military attache at that time in Prague?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He attended those meetings, Mr. Milosevic. Whether he was still there in capacity of military attache to Czechoslovakia, whether he had been replaced by that time, I don't know and I'm not interested, but the fact remains that Colonel Zimonja was present at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Tell me this, then: Let's go back to your assignments. Your first assignment, as you yourself say, was to spy on your colleagues, fellow students, during the 1968 demonstrations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spying is an ugly word. The term we used was we infiltrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I agree that it's a very ugly word, but that is the contents of substance, as I understand it, of your work entailed. As you were a student and as your statement -- and until yesterday morning you were a protected witness at that, it has been redacted and I wasn't able to see what faculty you graduated from, where and when.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Philosophy, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What group?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: For your first assignment and from the time you began your work, were you paid for it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a moment ago you said you were delighted with the work you were doing, and when we make up this whole picture we now see that you were paid for your work. So the basic motive -- or rather, the motive for your involvement was money; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your motive, then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Purely ideological.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how much of it was ideological, how much was it lucrative?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, money wasn't important for me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday we heard from you that you received a new identity here, a new country of residence, and so on and so forth. I assume that you were given money too. So in this situation and in this particular instance, the motive wasn't a new identity and money, but it was ideological; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, Mr. Milosevic, if I were to have to say why I did what I did, fully disclosing my personality as just an attempt to establish the truth of the events that took place in 1991 that I was present at, and my identity, where I am residing, is completely irrelevant to this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that it is irrelevant, but what I'm asking you is this: How far was the motive of, how shall I put it, the material side, material gain, relevant, the material gain that stems from a new identity, a new country of residence, I assume a new job, for you and your family? Although it is irrelevant, as you yourself say, with respect to your testimony, but how relevant is it as a motive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at this point in my life, I am living from one salary, pay cheque, to another, so if you are trying to insinuate that somebody has paid me a large sum of money for me to appear here today, you're quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Lazarevic. So to all intents and purposes, as you began doing this in your student days, this was your in early youth and you spent your entire life, as you yourself claim and state, working, spying on your colleagues, fellow students to begin with, then you spied on your colleagues from work, I can see from the rest of the explanations you gave here, and finally, you spied on your co-combatants, your fellow fighters, during the war in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's something lacking there in your question, and that is who issued the orders to me to spy. I did not work for some minor service. I worked for the intelligence service of Yugoslavia, working on Yugoslavia's internal and external security. So to say that I was a spy is not quite logical in that sense, because I was in fact working for my own country, the country that you yourself belonged to at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm asking you, Mr. Lazarevic, precisely because I find it strange that somebody was working in KOS and that nobody knows him in KOS, nobody knows about him, including, in 1995, the man who you refer to constantly. You say in your statement that for a period of time you were in London. Did you spend some time in Canada?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were never in Canada?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And while in London, you were in charge of the Serb emigres there; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me: Your impressions at that time and your opinions now, how far was the Serb emigre population nationalistic at all, nationalistically disposed? How far was it a political opposition to the present authorities in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a very minimum extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. A very minimum extent.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is your impression? How far were the Serbs anyway anti-Croat disposed at all and were they ever anti-disposed against the Croatians or Croats? Did you ever feel that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when you were spying on the Serb emigres.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the object of my assignment. The object of my assignment was to find who was in the leadership of those organisations and what their future plans were, if they had any, and whether they had any links with the emigres or other emigres or, rather, people within Yugoslavia, not whether they were anti-Croat disposed. Actually, at that time, they were anti-Tito.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean anti-regime. They weren't anti-Croat or anti-anything else, they weren't confronted on that basis with anyone; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, was there any nationalism and nationalist confrontation in what you saw with the Croatian emigres? And I'm thinking of the Ustasha emigres.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was very strong and very pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You say very pronounced.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the role played by the Croatian Ustasha emigres in the events that took place before the break-up of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm partially aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far was this anti-Serb feeling which otherwise burgeoned in Croatia in 1989 and 1990, prior to the elections and after the elections, how far was that -- did that have its influence on the Ustasha emigres and how much did they wield influence on the citizens and political parties, et cetera? So how far did this sentiment affect the Serbs not only in the Krajina but all over Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about any of the Croatian emblems, the chequerboard emblem, radio stations, singing of songs or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not only talking about those emblems and the singing of nationalistic songs, although I do mean that too. I'm talking about dismissals from work, placing mines and bombs in apartments and houses, the killings, the fact that people were taken off, and something that the Croatian press is quite freely writing about today. I'm sure you read the Croatian press. And there's talk of that quite openly now and discussions that are being held there now. So everything that went on along these lines, did that have any affect and influence on the Serbs, not only in the Krajina but throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, because you say you worked for KOS, so do you know just how many members of the Ustasha emigres at the end of 1989 and beginning of 1990 returned to Croatia, and how far they wielded an influence on official Croatian policy and the policy towards the Serbs, first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have some knowledge, but it would be ludicrous if you thought that I knew everything. Unfortunately, I don't know everything, although I would have liked to have known everything. But the fact is that I did know some of the members of the Ustasha emigres who were present in the areas I moved around in, and specifically, for example, the leader, or rather, the commander of Karlovac. One of the Brate Brajdic and two others that had come in from Sweden. They were well known people in the very rigid stance they had towards Serbs and Serbs in Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The brothers you mentioned that had come from Sweden that were rampant in those parts, you say you don't know much about them, because, as far as I was able to understand, you were in Topusko and Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velika Kladusa, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, before the conflict in Velika Kladusa, and after that in Topusko and Vojnic. So you don't know much about the events that I'm asking you about, because you weren't -- you couldn't have known and seen everything from where you were.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly I got my information from others. At some of these events I was present myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, from your positions in Velika Kladusa and Vojnic, you have a whole image and picture of the state of affairs in the Republic of Srpska Krajina about the alleged Serb crimes, about all kinds of, as far as I was able to hear from you yesterday, crimes that were committed and the casualties of those crimes. You were an interpreter, you say, and as such a liaison officer with the UN, so how were you able, from that position and that place, to have all these myriad information that we heard about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information I presented yesterday relates to the period from February 1992 until August 1995, when I was the liaison officer, which meant that I was in constant contacts with the United Nations commands on the territory of the 21st Banija Corps. So most of those reports were accessible to me on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is from those UN reports, is it, that you draw your conclusions, you deduce, if I can put it that way, and bring conclusions as to the political intentions and political leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, of Serbia itself, of Yugoslavia, of the general political state of affairs, the military state of affairs and all the rest of it? Is that the basis from which you drew all this information, all your explanations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at no point that the groundwork and foundations of my knowledge were United Nations reports. Most of the events that I describe I was present at myself, personally, and the events that were talked about during the briefings, early-morning briefings at my command and headquarters. So it was a compilation of knowledge and information, not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. only from a single source, but from a number of sources, including my own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. How come in those personal experiences of yours there is nothing -- I don't wish to make a comparison, but for instance, we had here a journalist. His name was Jovan Dulovic. He also knew nothing about the great crimes that were perpetrated against the Serbs, for example. So you too have nothing and know nothing about the crimes perpetrated against the Serbs, but you explain here and give explanations to the effect that Serbs were criminals, thieves, that they burnt houses, tortured, that they set mines; that they didn't want anything that was good. They didn't want peace, they didn't want a truce of any kind, that they undermined each and every initiative to move forward. How come you make that kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is an inaccurate characterisation of what the witness testified to yesterday, and I don't see a question being posed to the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reformulate that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The thousands of Serbs that were killed, did the Serbs themselves kill them? Because you say and said a moment ago they were responsible for 80 per cent of their own victims in the Krajina between 1992 and 1995. Or was this committed, these crimes perpetrated by the revamped Ustasha movement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said, it refers to the 21st Corps, Mr. Milosevic. They were not generalised figures. I spoke about an analysis of the deaths that occurred within the 21st Corps. These figures do not relate to the whole of the Balkans or of the RSK or Croatia or Serbia; I'm just talking about the territory that I was -- had operative assignments in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the figures just relate, as you say, to where you were, whereas all the other observations relate to the entirety of the events that took place in Yugoslavia, in Croatia, the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the Srpska Republic and Serbia proper; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what applies to Kordun. I never gave a general statement here that would cover everything, the entire territory. If I gave evidence, I talked about events where I was present personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us then turn to other issues. In 1984, as you claim yourself, you started, again on orders of KOS, working for Agrokomerc in Velika Kladusa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
