utterances.text: And you say that you were in charge of foreigners and that later on you switched and started working in the production area.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in research and development department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout the time, based on my information, you worked there as an interpreter, and your wife's name is Zorica?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can Mr. Milosevic state the reason why it's necessary to identify this man's wife, given the history of this witness? How is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but is he giving evidence in private session or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is in a unique situation in that he has been relocated. Unless there's some relevance to mentioning the wife's name, I would ask that the question be stricken, and if there is some relevance, that it be taken in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you explain the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, I am here challenging what the witness said, namely, that he went to work for Agrokomerc pursuant to KOS orders, that he started working -- because he started working as an interpreter there, he got that job through his own contacts, whereas his wife worked as a physical education teacher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we'll go into private session for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that Belgrade was already concerned at that time regarding the safety of Agrokomerc because it was already under the control of the Muslims at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it was portrayed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you say "Belgrade," are you referring to the federal government or Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Main Staff of the JNA and KOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And if there was a concern, do you think that the reason for that was that Agrokomerc was under the control of Bosnian Muslims, or was it because of the financial scandal that broke out and started shaking this huge company that was established in that area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into reasons for sending me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't go into these reasons; however, you stress the nationalist aspect and not the financial one that was well known in Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large amount of foreign nationals in Velika Kladusa, and that was quite an important piece of information at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A high number of foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are at the time for the break. Mr. Lazarevic, we're going to take a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We take the break for 20 minutes. During the break you're reminded not to discuss your evidence with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you'll continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say yourself that you followed the activities of Sulejman Ugljanin at the time in Velika Kladusa concerning the SDA, tell us, please: What was that party all about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. What do you mean, what was the party all about? What kind of a party the SDA was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a nationalist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to this nationalist character of this party, were there also elements of Islamic fundamentalism?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did Ugljanin meet with in Velika Kladusa area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And were any Serbs members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked in Velika Kladusa normally, legally, under your own legal name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us: How was it that you, as a Serb, were able to attend those meetings of the SDA in order to be able to follow Sulejman Ugljanin's activities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend private meetings of Sulejman Ugljanin, but I did attend public meetings that were held at the local soccer field. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you said yourself that you spent seven years there, using your own legal name, yesterday you described an event when you were in a cafe, and this was just prior to what you described as an assignment when you had to eliminate the emigres from Sweden, the brothers Brajdic, and then yesterday you told us that two officers entered the cafe, that they were drunk, if I understood you well, and that they said something about Greater Serbia, and in a way they got you involved in that and compromised you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you said was correct except for one thing: I wasn't present in a cafe where the attack was supposed to be carried out, but I was in another cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But at any rate, was it right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that two officers came in, they were drunk, and said something about the Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were two officers from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From the JNA. And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that this whole area where we are now will be Greater Serbia soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what you said yesterday and this is what is contained in your statement regarding that event. This is on page 7. You said that: "I happened to be in a cafe on the 21st of December, 1991, three days prior to the planned ambush, when a captain entered the bar wearing a JNA uniform, completely drunk. As he entered, he started yelling, 'Brother Serb.' It was clear that he was addressing me because I was the only Serb in that establishment. I tried to ignore him, but it didn't fool anyone. I immediately left the bar, went back home, and through -- contacted police station in Vojnic on the radio. I told Ajdinovic what had happened. He told me to go and calm down the captain and that he would send someone to collect him," and so on. So yesterday you said that two people came and spoke about the Greater Serbia, and in your statement you say that it was the JNA captain who came in, drunk, and said to you, Brother Serb, "Brate Srbine." In Velika Kladusa, everyone knew that you were a Serb - you just told us that you used your legal name - so how could this have compromised you when he called you Brother Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't just call me Brother Serb. He also kissed me and then he spoke how all of this will be Serbia one day. And I simply completed what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But isn't it clear that there is a great difference between what you wrote in your statement and what you said here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any great discrepancy here. I just see that I added some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that the details are the difference between one captain or two drunk officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said two officers in my statement three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your statement here reflects just one person and one captain, so are you saying that this is another mistake in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no mistake in my statement. I spoke about two drunk officers. It is possible that later on, when the statement was translated, there was an error made, but I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lazarevic. Tell me, please: How did you come to leave Agrokomerc?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was accused of taking some documents from the office of Mr. Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That you took some documents from the office of Mr. Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you were fired from Agrokomerc due to some debts that amounted to 30.000 German marks and that when -- and that you fled in 1991 to the village of Gejkovac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely not correct. Upon leaving Agrokomerc, I remained in Velika Kladusa for that entire year, working in my own company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, and Witness, I can sense that the speed is working a hardship for the interpreters, so you must observe a pause between question and answer, both of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sincerely apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't spend three months in the home of the Lakic family?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lakic family? I never heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please: Is it true that you had -- you owed 2.000 German marks to Toso Pajic, and to Djuro Skaljac you owed 1.500, and to another person 3.000 German marks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the beginning of 1990, you established your own company, for which you say was financed by KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does "partially" mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Partially" means that part of the equipment was paid by the JNA money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1990, beginning of 1991, KOS left you alone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood that you started working on your own free will, based on what you just told us, and now you're telling us that they left you alone. Does that mean that prior to that they harassed you, or does this "leaving alone" mean something else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working for KOS was no harassment at all. It was part of my nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 6 you describe an alleged meeting that you had in Vojnic at the police station with Zimonja, Ajdinovic, Pajic, and Lukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Lukic; Skaljac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, do you have the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we should have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd also ask that witness be provided a copy. It's a lengthy statement and seems unfair for him to be asked particular sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one copy here. I'll have somebody photocopy -- copies for the Chamber and we should have them in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would ask that Mr. Milosevic please tell us is it the Serbian copy or the English copy when he refers to a particular page number. It will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you again: Isn't it true that at that time Zimonja was a military attache in Prague?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. All I know is that he attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say at the police station in this line of untruths that you are saying here, none of these people had any status in the police force. Was that the military command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Toso Pajic was the chief of police in Vojnic, and Djuro Skaljac was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Answer me: Was it the military command pulled out from Karlovac because they were under constant siege and attack by Croatian paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a military command in Vojnic. It was in a different place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this Operative Group was pulled out of Karlovac where it was exposed to attacks by Croatian paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the task of the then command was to accept parts of the JNA that had been blocked in barracks in Jastrebarsko, Karlovac, and Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these events that you are mentioning, Mr. Milosevic, happened before I moved to the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that Zimonja, who was then in Czechoslovakia, said that Croatians and Muslims are working together to establish paramilitary groups and that these groups are a greater threat to civilians than to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the report that I made, it said lesser threat, not greater. I remember that I did not attach great importance to those elements in Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that you felt yourself that it was your patriotic duty to help the organisation of the self-defence of Serb civilians. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always felt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the threat to them exactly when they needed to organise self-defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishment of very nationalist parties, such as the SDA and the HDZ, which did not conceal their animosity to the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean unequivocally, then, that Serbs in Krajina and in this area of Zazine were jeopardised by the rising Croatian and Muslim nationalism?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You assert that at that meeting the plan of attack on Cetingrad was also discussed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as you say, Ajdinovic advocated that everybody should be locked up and killed by shelling. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in Cetingrad there were no Serbs at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to Serbs from Cetingrad? Were they expelled?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I don't know about any Serbs being in Cetingrad at all at the time I'm speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you got the task to form a secret group at that meeting, which you say consisted of you, Mile Bosnic and a person named Zeljko, who you know nothing else about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not about forming a secret group. It was about organising Serbs in Velika Kladusa for any contingency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of Serb it is if you don't know anything but his name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about Mile Bosnic. His wife was a hairdresser. This Zeljko person was a driver to Mile Bosnic and he had no major role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, you said that at the police station in Vojnic you were issued with equipment and weapons for this secret group.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The weapons were issued for a specific assignment we got.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which specific assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elimination of Ustasha emigres and those helping them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to carry out the task?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and two JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the assignment where your cover was blown by somebody telling you "Brother Serb" in a cafe?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. There are more details that I didn't mention in the incident when they entered the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could they have blown your cover if you had lived in Velika Kladusa for a long time by then and everybody knew you were a Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't active politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And by addressing you as Brother Serb, he proclaimed you politically active; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were supposed to distribute weapons to them and see them every day. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons I received were issued for my use, and it was stored at the apartment where I lived. And who was I supposed to meet on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking on the basis of your statement. You got three rifles. They were not all for your personal use, were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got one Scorpio with a muffler, an automatic rifle with two cartridges, a pistol, and four hand grenades. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These rifles mentioned in the statement, you didn't get?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic received them for other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Look up your own statement and you will see it is not correct either.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll find it. Give me a second. I'm sorry to waste time in this way, but ... Here it is, on page 7. "In this period I was invited to the police station in Vojnic." The beginning of page 7. "At the police station in Vojnic I was issued with weapons and other equipment; a Scorpion with silencer, three automatic rifles (Yugoslav version of AK-47), a pistol, four hand grenades, ammunition, and two Motorola radios. All of these things were given to me in a bag by a uniformed policeman as I left the station. I was told that I should notify Bosnic and Zeljko, last name unknown, to be ready to go into action should I contact them. I was to distribute weapons to them and I was supposed to meet with each of them at least once a day to see if they had heard or seen anything suspicious. If they had, I was to report it to Vojnic. Otherwise, I was told to return to Velika Kladusa and await further instructions." End of your quotation. Of your statement, by the way. You claim it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this statement is correct. But, Mr. Milosevic, two minutes ago when you asked the question, you asked me: Did you meet with them every day? And I was assuming that you were talking about JNA officers who were supposed to carry out that assignment, because that question seemed to refer to that statement which was actually never carried out. Mr. Bosnic was a family friend and I could have seen him every day. And his driver as well, because he was always with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted this because you said earlier that those three rifles were received by you for your own personal use, and I asked what for, and you said it was not correct.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat again what I said. I said I got a pistol with a muffler for my own personal use, rifles, four hand grenades, two Motorolas, et cetera. The three automatic rifles mentioned in my statement were given to Bosnic for other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you read this differently? It says here, "I was invited to Vojnic and at the Vojnic police station I was issued with weapons and other equipment; a Skorpion with silencer, three automatic rifles, a pistol, four hand grenades, ammunition, and two Motorolas."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So where is the difference between your statement and my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is not my statement. You say that you did not receive three rifles.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's rewind a little. You say that I got it for my personal use and I'm saying that they were given and intended for Mile Bosnic; Motorolas, hand grenades, a pistol, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you also got rifles.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but they were given to Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago the rifles were given to someone else, not you. You can look up the transcript later. I don't want to waste time over this. Tell me one other thing: What was the name of that policeman who issued you with these weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that somebody issued these weapons and equipment at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You describe the attack on Cetingrad.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, what date did the attack happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was late October. In 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who made or who could have made the decision to attack Cetingrad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said it was made by Ajdinovic, Pajic, Skaljac, and Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They made the recommendation to the General Staff of the JNA in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the decision on that attack was made by the headquarters of the Territorial Defence that was in Vojnic at the time, whereas Vojnic was not in the RSK at all at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the Territorial Defence had anything to do with if. Did they have artillery or was the artillery in the hands of the JNA? All I know is that two high-ranking officers of the JNA analysed the situation on the ground, submitted their report to the General Staff in Belgrade, and then the attack followed. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Lazarevic. If you had only read newspapers from that time, or if you had only asked anyone, you would know now that it is not true. The attack on Cetingrad was on the 28th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are talking about things that happened 12 years ago. You can't expect me to remember the exact date, hour, minute and the rest. All I know, it was cold, it was winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. The fact that this piece of information you quoted is incorrect has no importance, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite true. I know the event happened. I was there. Whether it was in late October or in November is not so important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was on the 28th November. Anyway, why did the attack happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the attack was caused by the fact that paramilitary formations in Cetingrad, several days before the attack, killed Lieutenant Colonel Rankovic and later, out of fear, and almost without a fight, left Cetingrad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's interesting, because the information I had was that this lieutenant colonel was killed with a bullet in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Cetingrad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- I heard that he was killed by Serbian forces. Intentionally or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was not killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed outside of Cetingrad, and the medical report said that the bullets came from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then Croats, after the matter of Rankovic, left Cetingrad almost without a fight, because Serbs had killed him.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that Rankovic was killed by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything. Those were the rumours, the stories that made the rounds. Mr. Milosevic and Your Honours, I want to state very clearly once again: My testimony refers to events which I attended personally and not events that happened in Cetingrad while I was in Velika Kladusa. I can't give you any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you still speak about it. You refer to it in your statement. You can't say now that you know nothing about it. You said that Zimonja's plan was favoured and accepted and the corridor was left for the population of Cetingrad to leave.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was the last time you were in Cetingrad before the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never really was in Cetingrad. I was in transit towards Plitvice twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you say it was undefended except for perhaps a few men with small arms? How can you say that when you have no direct knowledge, as you say now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talk about things that I heard on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you heard about it. And tell me: Who were the people who defended Cetingrad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was defended at all. I keep saying that the attack was carried out. I know I was standing on a hilltop with a group of other people, that we were watching the explosions in the skies, and that the inflow from Cetingrad into Velika Kladusa ensued after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was this -- who were these men who ran away to Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were armed, some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the extent of destruction in Cetingrad and the amount of casualties? Do you have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't take part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Brajdic brothers, whom you mentioned as Croatian extremists from Croatia, also flee Cetingrad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in mid-December 1991, you got the assignment to kill them; is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Them and anyone else who happened to be in the cafe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you explain -- a very simple question here: How can you explain that you, as an interpreter, a civilian, got an assignment to kill someone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think of myself only as an interpreter or a civilian in those events, one; and second, the assignment I received boiled down to the fact that I was on the ground at the time, that I was familiar with that part of Velika Kladusa, that I was familiar with the persons in question, and I was supposed to be one of a threesome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that this threesome was formed and you were one of this threesome to commit a murder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. You are putting things in a different context, and I can't explain it. It is a fact that the task was issued to eliminate someone. It is also a fact that it never happened. Another fact is that I left Velika Kladusa before anything happened, and eventually the assignment was never carried out. And in any case, I would have found a pretext to avoid it, whatever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you accepted this assignment and a threesome for liquidation was formed, of which you were a member.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say, on page 8, paragraph 5, that some ten days later, another unknown officer, more precisely, a military policeman of the JNA, drove you to Samarica, in Banija, an isolated and very safe place in a national park between Petrinja and Bosanski Novi, which served as headquarters, operative headquarters of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find this paragraph. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm still looking. It would be of very great help to me if Mr. Milosevic would actually tell me which page I'm searching for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 8, paragraph 5, but I haven't found it in my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is Mr. Milosevic referring to the Serbian version or the English version? Because the pagination will differ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it the Serbian version, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the Serbian version, yes. Second paragraph from the top, page 8. "After these ten days passed, a military policeman showed up and told me to go with him. We drove to Samarica, in Banija, which was the headquarters of the JNA 8th Operational Group."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's page 9 in the English text, the beginning of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got it, Your Honour. I'm reading it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that it was very secure and it was a place between Petrinja and Bosanski Novi. "It was very secure and served as the JNA's operational headquarters for the northern part of Croatia," and so on and so forth. Now, the headquarters of the operational group -- have you found it, Mr. Lazarevic? Have you found the passage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I found your version and now I'm looking at the English version that I have before me here. [In English] So what is the question? [Interpretation] So what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is the following, Mr. Lazarevic: Once again you are thinking things up, because the headquarters of the 8th Operational Group was not at Samarica but at Petrova Gora. So why are you speaking untruths?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February, March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely when you say that the headquarters of the 8th Operational Group was at Petrova Gora and not at Samarica, and there are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents to bear that up.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was told that it was at Samarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Quite obviously you have very characteristic answers when you're not telling the truth. You go on to say the following: Thanks to Zimonja at the time, you suddenly became a lieutenant colonel, got that rank. Is that what it says, "suddenly," in my report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I'm asking you: Suddenly you were accorded a rank, and it was lieutenant colonel of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, let us know the page to which you refer in the statement so that we can follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about that same paragraph, Mr. Robinson, and this is what he says: "I was given a uniform with a JNA's lieutenant colonel's rank," and in brackets, "As later to become the RSK army." "And given a room in a house at the headquarters. Zimonja was not present but it was obvious that he was responsible for my preferential treatment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you know that two civilian persons with a university degree, whether they be doctors or interpreters, engineers or whatever, professionals in their field, they're always given some military rank by way of status, to denote their status, even interpreters, who went as civilians sometimes to the United Nations detachments, they would get ranks too, the rank of lieutenant or whatever, to give them some sort of status. So they weren't actually soldiers, the rank and file, but officers. So you, as an interpreter, were given this rank as a designation and not as an actual position and rank in the headquarters. You performed the function of an interpreter for English because you spoke English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have any command functions at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were a liaison officer - that was your function - with people who speak the same language as you do yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time -- let me first ask you: Was Bulat the commander there and then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did you hear him talk to Perisic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you claim that the army of Republika Srpska was formed from the JNA, or rather, that the JNA became the RS army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the equipment and manpower, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When the JNA withdrew from Croatia, JNA members stayed on there who were from the region; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were from Belgrade and you were an interpreter; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A liaison officer with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the ECMM, and the Red Cross, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So with international organisations.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right, Mr. Milosevic. That's what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what I'm saying is the officers that were from the Krajina stayed on in Krajina to form the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you claim that the army of Republika Srpska Krajina was part of the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of its formation, by virtue of the orders it received, by virtue of the fact that it had brought in the convoy, equipped it with weapons, fuel, food, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's distinguish here between some sort of assistance from actual command, the function of command. Do you claim that the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia was in command of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the General Staff of the JNA was in command of the officers who were serving their time in the Krajina region and in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you claim that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was a constant link between the General Staff of the army in Belgrade and the headquarters of the Krajina army, and Belgrade paid the officers directly from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave aside material assistance and remuneration. Do you claim - and please give me a very precise answer - that the army of Republika Srpska Krajina was part of the Yugoslav army, the army of Yugoslavia, and that the General Staff of the JNA commanded the army of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that that is a lie, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I consider that to be a greater truth than the truth of you and me sitting here, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This characterisation of this witness's testimony as a lie is improper comment and is not a question posed to this witness. He asked the witness his opinion regarding a matter, and the witness replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's entitled to put it to him that he's telling a lie. It's for the witness to answer. Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina had its headquarters, its main staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Republic of Srpska Krajina had its supreme defence council?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what connection did the supreme defence council of the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina have with the General Staff of the JNA or the supreme defence council of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the chain of command, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, never were you able to see this kind of chain of command and identify it because it simply didn't exist. How are you able to make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat to this Tribunal every -- it was in contact with the JNA and headquarters from Belgrade, the officers that came from Belgrade on a daily basis practically, and the ones that left the Krajina went to Belgrade and the new contingent coming from Belgrade was a constant supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You even said yesterday that officers were coming to replace each other on a six-month basis.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the officers who were members of the JNA remained there and became part of the structure of the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina? They were there throughout the war, they remained there, and nobody went to and fro, from Belgrade and the Krajina, or replaced each other after six-month term of office, and the people you mentioned didn't leave after six months, they were there all the time, because they were people from the Krajina originally; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not correct there. You're partially right but not right in all things because you know full well, just like I do, that the General Staff of the JNA would send officers regularly to do a six-month term of office by virtue of the place they were born in and then they would be returned to their own commands regardless of where they were. You know that and I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what I know is something that is quite contrary to what you know, and that is what I'm saying that I'm saying and asking you the questions I'm asking you. Of course, we will have every opportunity to clarify the matter fully in due course. So is it not true that just a part of the officer corps of the JNA, that is to say those who were from the region originally, after the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia remained on in the Krajina and became active members of the army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command component of the army of the RSK was made up by active officers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Active officers. They continued wearing a uniform upon their return to Belgrade in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are getting French. Can it be resolved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, Mr. Milosevic. Let's try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, on page 8, paragraph 6, that at the beginning of 1992, Samarica was visited by Zimonja and said that the JNA said -- would withdraw from Croatia to Bosnia and that Belgrade had approved for the European Community Monitoring Mission, the ECMM, to enter into the area from Sisak and Karlovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Belgrade," I assume you mean the presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zimonja used the word "Belgrade" and I always assumed that he meant the Main Staff, the General Staff, and not the political structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you know that the civilian structures at that time, the Presidency of the SFRY, as it was called, was in command of the army and was the collective supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not assume anything, Mr. Milosevic. I'm just saying with great certainty what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what you state, the withdrawal of the JNA and all rest of it, all the other things you state, does that mean that the peace plan was respected, both in the military and political sense, and that the SFRY and the JNA demonstrated that there were no aggressive intentions vis-a-vis Croatia, and that was all according to the Vance plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, part of the JNA did withdraw. It is an indisputable fact that that same army, the JNA, left its officers behind to form the army of the RSK and that it left its heavy weaponry there for that army to use; therefore, yes, the plan was partially fulfilled, Mr. Milosevic, but not completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, Mr. Lazarevic: As the JNA was composed of - while Yugoslavia existed I'm talking about - of the citizens from all the republics, when the crisis started and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia established, its citizens or, rather, the citizens of Serbia and Montenegro returned to the territory of that same Yugoslavia. Similarly, the citizens of Serb ethnicity in the Republika Srpska Krajina stayed on on their territory, so also did the citizens of Croatian nationality stay on and formed the command cadres of their armed forces, so Muslim officers that had once been in the JNA remained in their own locality and became commanders of the Muslim army. All right. Let's not mention the Mujahedin now and anybody else from outside. I'm just talking about the internal elements and factors. Does that mean that the JNA formed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're speaking too --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Rule of thumb: Any time you exceed three or four sentences, it's going to be difficult for the witness to answer. Formulate a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Did the same thing happen with the Croatian officers who remained officers in the armed forces of Croatia, or the officers who remained in the armed forces of the Bosnian Croats or the remaining officers who stayed on in Alija Izetbegovic's army, did the JNA form all those armies, establish them all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an essential, substantial difference once again, and Mr. Milosevic, you're only partially right. It is true that the redistribution of the JNA meant that the Croatian officers joined the Croatian army, the Bosnian officers joined the Bosnian army. However, in none of these cases did the JNA of its own free will leave its weaponry and officers, for example, in Croatia, nor after the dismemberment were there any contacts between those armies and the General Staff in Belgrade, whereas there were daily contacts between the officers of the RSK army with Belgrade. That is why I say you're partially right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have absolutely no possibility of knowing about any type of daily contact that was held between officers and the General Staff in Belgrade. I assume that they must have had daily contact with the Supreme Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Command of the army of RSK and not with the General Staff in Belgrade. And even if were such a vertical chain of command and line to be organised, it had to go through the main headquarters of the ARSK because, otherwise, it couldn't have happened and wouldn't have happened in any other army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it happened in this particular army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to say how many JNA officers were left behind to form the RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would place it at a hundred per cent for the high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All of the high-ranking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes; all the generals and all the colonels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, were all these officers who stayed behind, who remained, were they all from that region originally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they stayed on in their own territory, on their own land, in their own towns and villages where they had come from, in the areas they were born and lived their whole life, their fathers and grandfathers lived in that locality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is illusory for you to try to claim that I met all the officers on the territory of Srpska Krajina. I just spoke about the ones that I had known. Whether they were all born and bred there, I really can't say. The ones that I knew, yes, they were. The ones that I knew were born there, they left the region, might not have been there for 40 or 50 years and then came back on assignment when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think they were given an assignment to go back or did they feel the need to go back, just like you said that you felt it to be your patriotic duty to defend and protect this area, just like the officers who had gone through an officer's training course, felt that same duty just the kind of duty that you felt yourself, or were they ordered by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Milosevic, not everybody was a patriot. Some people came for very selfish reasons, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said for selfish reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into those selfish reasons now. I haven't got time for that. But tell me this: Zimonja, on that occasion when he said that the JNA was withdrawing from Croatia, et cetera, et cetera, he said to you that you would be following Mile Mrksic, accompanying him, who, as you say, was the commander of the 8th Operative Group at the time, when you went to meetings with the observers; right? So how many meetings did you attend of that kind with Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably about 20, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in what capacity did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an interpreter to General Mrksic, because the liaison officer at that time was Colonel Momcilo Krstic. I was his assistant, his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Precisely so. So at those meetings you were not accompanying Mile Mrksic actually but you were accompanying the liaison officer who, from time to time, would invite you to attend meetings of that kind in your capacity of interpreter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. -- or rather, General Krstic didn't speak a single language except Serbian, and neither did General Mrksic. So when the liaison officer attended meetings that were attended by General Mrksic, I would also be there as an assistant to help out as an interpreter to the general and not to Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your capacity as interpreter.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, in a large portion of your statement, on page 9, 10, 11 -- you can find it there. Anyway, in those pages you describe how you allegedly fooled the representatives of the UN and the observers, how you tried to recruit them to -- tried to do business with them, get them drunk, you supplied women to them, extracted information from them, and so on. So tell me, please: Since everything that we heard yesterday is completely untrue, how can we at all verify -- how is it possible at all to verify any one of your allegations that can be found throughout these pages of your statement, except for the story of yours -- once you sift through the story, the only fact that remains is that you were an interpreter, and you have a very eloquently told story. So you are coming up with big items here, that you used to get the UN representatives drunk, that you used to do business with them, supply them with women, extract information from them. So how is it possible to come up with some allegations which are quite large?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be possible to go into the closed session where I can actually name the names of the people that I worked with on the part of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, he is not testifying in a closed session. I don't see the reason for a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have made that judgement. Closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to you saying how you recruited them, got them drunk, bribed them, did business with them, supplied them with women and so on, in another part you say that some representatives of the UN and monitoring mission after a while started cooperating not out of those low-based motives but because they became convinced of the valid cause of the Serb struggle.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was done out of their convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you said how you deceived them, did you in fact deceive them regarding the valid cause of the Serb struggle?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I never lectured officers of the UN in order to make them believe this or that. Those who made conclusions based on their own convictions did so on their own free will, without any influence of mine. You are suggesting that I in fact had a much greater power than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm claiming something completely contrary to that, because based on what you're saying, it seems that you know everything about the war in Croatia, about the policy of Yugoslavia, Serbia, my own role, the role of the Main Staff, and everything else, when in fact you know nothing about this because you were an interpreter in the command where you worked as a liaison officer. You in fact fabricated all this. So, Mr. Lazarevic, I'm claiming something completely opposite of what you are saying. I'm not saying that you know everything, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness comment on that. It has been said that this is an entire fabrication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will repeat again, Your Honour, for the benefit of the Court here: Everything I have stated in my statements is absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, on page 9, last paragraph, you say that Mrksic, while he was still in the Krajina, told you about his impressions from the Vukovar battlefield, and he confided in you regarding all of that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never claimed that, Mr. Milosevic. I simply said that I was present when he spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did he in fact say there about doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His conviction at the time was that he had accomplished a very important military victory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that he boasted about this - this is the term that you used - he boasted about something that was dishonourable; he boasted about killing a civilian - is that what he did? - about ordering a crime to be carried out or something similar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He boasted about having accomplished what he wanted in his attack on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps tempted to ask him how many Croatian extremists, Ustashas, members of the ZNG, and other organisations, withdrew after the surrender of Vukovar and dressed into medical staff clothing in order to portray themselves as the medical staff and the wounded? Did you then ask him how many Serbs these Ustasha groups killed at the time in Vukovar? Did you have information regarding that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was not in a position to put questions to General Mrksic. I was there, the dinner was going on, members of the command were there, officers talked amongst themselves. I was sitting nearby and I was able to hear, however, I did not actually participate in the conversation and I don't know everything that went on in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what went on in Vukovar, but this is what you're giving evidence about. Do you know that it is exactly Mile Mrksic -- were you able to eavesdrop about this while they were talking at the table?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I wasn't eavesdropping, I was sitting there in an official capacity while the dinner was going on. I was not eavesdropping. I was sitting there and I was able to hear something that was said quite loudly. I wasn't there, listening to something that I wasn't supposed to hear. Mr. Mrksic loud and clearly said about his impressions from Vukovar, so I wasn't eavesdropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the waiter who waited there was also there in an official capacity, and let's say he was serving soup, and since he has ears, he was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The waiter was a military personnel person, just like I was, and was present there in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that Mile Mrksic, regarding not only Serbs but Croats who remained to live in the Krajina area, organised medical health care services for them, that in fact he took care of the health of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. population living there? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you said in your statement, and also in your evidence, that Serbs, the TO of Krajina, the police of Krajina, all of those people who were armed and those who were not armed, worked actively on expelling all Croats from that area. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the impression I got upon arriving in Krajina, and I put that in my statement. I said that when I came to Krajina there was a very small number of Croats living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take a look at my notes. Just a minute, please. Therefore, in view of the fact that everyone was supposed to be expelled from there, tell me, please: Do you know of a village called Bijeljina, which is some ten kilometres from Topusko?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that 37 Croatian families remained to live in that village, that they spent the entire war on their property, and only those who set on fire Serb houses fled from there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about only one village near Topusko. I think that I mentioned this in my statement that there were Croats in Topusko who put white sheets on their windows, and they remained living in Topusko. I don't know if it's the same village that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It might not have been the same village. There were many villages like that. Do you know in fact that Croats lived in Knin, in Knin itself, and according to a protected witness, a very important one whose name I don't want to mention now, this witness personally saw them and believed that they were given equal treatment in every respect, even though this witness testified against me, just like you. So there were Croats in Knin itself. All right. You don't know about this village, but do you know how many Croatian families remain in the village of Gredjani?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that village because the members of the ECMM visited this area very frequently. I believe that this is a village on the Kupa River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the Muza family, Slavko and Kata, from Topusko, since you visited Topusko? And I'm asking you now about Topusko.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the soldiers of the RSK, who tried to provoke them because their son, Ivica Muza, also known as Svabo, that was his nickname, set fire to Serb houses, so therefore the Serb soldiers provoked the parents of this arsonist, and pursuant to the order of Ajdinovic, whom you accuse of commanding a unit in charge of dirty jobs, that these soldiers were arrested because they harassed this Croatian family? Do you know about this event?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that Ajdinovic commanded this unit that did dirty jobs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of Croatian villages called Lukinic, Buncici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are now mentioning villages that probably exist in that area. I'm not a person from that area. I did spend a part of my life in that area; however, I didn't study geography. I don't know about all of these villages. I didn't record these villages and their population. I don't know what the ethnic composition of these villages is. This was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But part of your job is quite clear to us, based on what you're saying. I am now giving you names of a number of villages from the area where you claim to know everything that went on, and it seems that you know nothing of what went on except for things that corroborate this false accusation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are saying now that I'm lying and you are saying the truth. I can turn it around and say that it's vice versa. I'm quite sincerely telling you that I don't know. I've never heard of these villages that you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that what I say to you about Lukinic, Buncici, residents of those villages who lived throughout the war there peacefully, I also mentioned Bjeljevina, Gredjani, and these villages, and you're claiming that that's a lie?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm claiming that there were no Croats living peacefully at that time in RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, there was nobody living peacefully in Krajina during the war. You're not going to deny that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to deny that. It is true that nobody lived peacefully, especially not Croats during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as regards the truth, the only advantage I have is that I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will leave it to the Court to decided who is telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I am saying is something that a lot of people know a lot about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the same about what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, when I say a lot of people, I mean millions. On page 12, paragraph 5, you say that after demilitarisation, and nothing changed, and that the KOS and DB remained active in RSK. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the army, overnight --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I took you to say that KOS was part of the JNA army, and the DB from Serbia, that they remained there and continued working in RSK.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the army of RSK had its own intelligence and counter-intelligence service, even before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Every republic had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that at the level of RSK there was their own state security service?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was directly subordinated to the state security of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you claim that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They submitted their reports to them, they asked for advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any report of that nature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any reports, but I had an opportunity to talk to the people who worked in the state security of RSK and had direct connection with Mr. Stanisic, or Stamatovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you ever attend a meeting? Have you ever seen Jovica Stanisic in your life?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did he meet with there? Did you see?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, Mr. Martic; a number of people. I attended dinners, not official conversation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what if he came for a visit and had dinner? What are you testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You only asked whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is your testimony when I ask did you ever attend a meeting between them? Because you're saying something about reporting as the grounds for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I was in the presence of Mr. Toso Pajic, in his office, many times when he spoke to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he giving him a report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you attended a telephone conversation between Toso Pajic and Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Pajic, Surla, and the others were working for the DB in the RSK, in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from that area, they are locals of that area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but they were still officers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA had ceased to exist when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came into existence and when the army of Yugoslavia was established, consisting of citizens of Montenegro and Serbia. I suppose that you are well informed about that as well, since you know a lot about things that you couldn't really know about. What is the presence of the Yugoslav army in the RSK you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the presence of units in the MUP of Serbia. What secret units are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean that the secret services of the MUP of Serbian Krajina cooperated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is odd about that cooperation? So what if they cooperated? You should know, since you work in that area, that secret services of the USA and Russia also have cooperation. There is cooperation between secret services of various states, even between Yugoslavia and the United States. So what if there is cooperation between such services?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends to what level this cooperation reaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's all about level; right? And I suppose you know the level of that cooperation as well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you know the substance of that cooperation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying all the things I know about that. I know that Mr. Toso Pajic talked to Stanisic. I know that upon return to Belgrade, Toso Pajic continued to work in the DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, after these events that you described towards the end of examination-in-chief, do you know that in Serbia there were a million refugees? Out of those million refugees, do you know how many thousands upon thousands found employment? Those who were policemen found work in the police force, doctors found work in health centres, teachers found employment in schools, depending on vacancies available. So what if a policeman who was at the same time a refugee after the events you described, found employment in the only line of work he knows anything about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You seem to forget, Mr. Milosevic, that at that time, people who came as refugees to the territory of Yugoslavia had no right to be issued with an ID, had no right to employment because they were considered as aliens, they could not enrol their children in schools because they had no official status in our country. So please don't tell me what rights they did and didn't have. I know that they were denied all the rights normally enjoyed by Yugoslav citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you know that many people who were driven out - and that was the general feeling in Serbia, beginning with the early 1990s - were in many ways privileged, as far as employment is concerned, compared to Yugoslav citizens? I know that Sadako Ogata told me that the status of refugees is very good in Serbia. Now you're telling me that these people were disenfranchised in Serbia, based on a single incident you mentioned here, and even that, I would say, is doubtful.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm speaking about the years I spent in Belgrade, from 1995, 1997, 1998, and 1999. The people I spoke to at the office of the exiled government of Serbian Krajina in Belgrade, I know from speaking to them that they had no rights at all. They were unable to register their vehicles they drove to Serbia. For years they were unable to be issued with IDs, because an ID would mean that they got Yugoslav citizenship. They couldn't do that. You cannot deny the fact that in 1995 those people were arrested and taken back to the war zone and battlefields outside of Serbia. You know, and you should tell the Court, that some of these people sued your government because you made those refugees go back to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, that is not true at all. There were all kinds of excesses there. There probably were. Whenever hundreds, thousands of people are involved, injustice and excess is a common occurrence. But it was not official policy. You can't claim that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It could only have happened in individual cases. But please tell me this: Since you say that services were cooperating between them, did you attend a single meeting, for instance, between Surla and Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't attend a meeting between Stanisic and Pajic either?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.
